title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 839–841 (Night 187, continuing nights-186), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 187 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Half-drowned and shaking with cold, the servant Ṣawāb begs to be let out of the well, and Qamar al-Zamān hauls him up and lets him go to change his clothes, on his promise to come back and tell the truth. Instead the servant runs straight to King Shahramān, who has lain awake fearing for his son in the old tower while the vizier counsels him to keep the prince locked up a month until his temper softens. The servant reports that the prince has lost his mind: he insists a girl spent the night with him and has beaten the servant to make him say who took her, though the door was locked all night and the key lay under the servant's head. The king cries out for his son, turns in fury on the vizier who advised the imprisonment, and sends him to find out what has happened. The vizier finds Qamar al-Zamān calmly reading the Qurʾan; when he hears what the servant has said of him, the prince flies into a rage and accuses them of having coached the servant. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-seventh night,
sentences.n: al-sābiʿa, “the seventh”, agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ قَالَ لِلْخَادِمِ وَاللَّهِ مَا أُطْلِعُكَ مِنْ هٰذِهِ الْبِئْرِ حَتَّى تُخْبِرَنِي بِخَبَرِ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَمَنِ الَّذِي أَخَذَهَا وَأَنَا نَائِمٌ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni qāla li-al-khādimi wa-Allāhi mā uṭliʿuka min hādhihi al-biʾri ḥattā tukhbiranī bi-khabari hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati wa-mani alladhī akhadhahā wa-anā nāʾimun
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān said to-the-servant: By-God, not I-bring-you-up from this the-well until you-tell-me with-(the)-news (of) this the-girl, and-who (is) the-one-who took-her while-I (was) sleeping.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān said to the servant, “By God, I will not bring you up out of this well until you tell me all about this girl, and who it was that took her away while I slept.”
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up the story by repeating, a little shortened, the threat with which the last night ended. mā uṭliʿuka, “I will not bring you up”: mā with the imperfect for a future denial is later usage; in the answer to an oath Classical Arabic would more usually say lā uṭliʿuka. biʾr, “well”, is feminine, hence hādhihi. ḥattā takes the subjunctive, tukhbiranī. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”: bi- marks the news told. The ئ of البئر and نائم is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ بَعْدَ مَا عَايَنَ الْمَوْتَ يَاسَيِّدِي أَطْلِقْنِي وَأَنَا أَحْكِي لَكَ عَلَى الصَّحِيحِ وَأُخْبِرُكَ بِالْخَبَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu baʿda mā ʿāyana al-mawta yā sayyidī aṭliqnī wa-anā aḥkī laka ʿalā al-ṣaḥīḥi wa-ukhbiruka bi-al-khabari
sentences.l: So-he-said to-him, after (that) he-had-seen-with-his-eyes the-death: O-my-master, release-me, and-I will-relate to-you according-to the-true-(account) and-tell-you with-the-news.
sentences.i: Then, having looked death in the face, the servant said to him, “My master, let me go, and I will tell you the truth of it and give you the whole story.”
sentences.n: baʿda mā, “after”, with a verb: mā turns the clause into a noun-like phrase, “after his seeing”. ʿāyana, Form III, “to see with one's own eyes”: he has seen death itself, not just feared it. The print runs يا and سيدي together, ياسيدي; the spacing is kept. aṭliqnī, Form IV imperative, “set me free”. wa-anā aḥkī, “and I will tell”: the wāw links a promise to the request, and the plain imperfect carries the future. ʿalā al-ṣaḥīḥ, “according to what is true”, that is, truthfully.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ جَذَبَهُ مِنَ الْبِئْرِ وَأَطْلَعَهُ وَهُوَ غَائِبٌ عَنِ الْوُجُودِ مِنْ شِدَّةِ مَا قَاسَاهُ مِنَ الْبَرْدِ وَالْعَذَابِ وَالْغِطَاسِ وَالْخَوْفِ مِنَ الْغَرَقِ وَالضَّرْبِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika jadhabahu mina al-biʾri wa-aṭlaʿahu wa-huwa ghāʾibun ʿani al-wujūdi min shiddati mā qāsāhu mina al-bardi wa-al-ʿadhābi wa-al-ghiṭāsi wa-al-khawfi mina al-gharaqi wa-al-ḍarbi
sentences.l: So-at that he-pulled-him from the-well and-brought-him-up, and-he (was) absent from the-existence from (the) severity (of) what he-had-suffered of the-cold and-the-torment and-the-dunking and-the-fear of the-drowning and-the-beating.
sentences.i: At that he hauled him out of the well and brought him up, and the man was senseless from the force of all he had suffered: the cold and the torment, the dunking, the fear of drowning, and the beating.
sentences.n: fa-ʿinda dhālika, “and at that”, the narrator's usual hinge between one action and the next. ghāʾib ʿan al-wujūd, “absent from existence”, means unconscious, lost to the world. min shiddati mā, “from the severity of what”: min gives the cause. qāsā, Form III, “to endure, suffer”. الغطاس is read al-ghiṭās, “dunking, immersion”, a later noun from ghaṭasa, “to plunge under water”, known from the Egyptian name of Epiphany, ʿīd al-ghiṭās; the vowels are a likely guess, not certain. gharaq, “drowning”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ يَرْتَعِدُ مِثْلَ الْقَصَبَةِ فِى الرِّيحِ الْعَاصِفِ وَاشْتَبَكَتْ أَسْنَانُهُ فِي بَعْضِهَا وَابْتَلَّتْ ثِيَابُهُ وَتَلَوَّثَ بَدَنُهُ وَتَشَطَّبَ مِنْ حِيطَانِ الْبِئْرِ وَصَارَ فِي حَالَةٍ شَنِيعَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra yartaʿidu mithla al-qaṣabati fī al-rīḥi al-ʿāṣifi wa-ishtabakat asnānuhu fī baʿḍihā wa-ibtallat thiyābuhu wa-talawwatha badanuhu wa-tashaṭṭaba min ḥīṭāni al-biʾri wa-ṣāra fī ḥālatin shanīʿatin
sentences.l: And-he-began trembling like the-reed in the-wind the-storming, and-locked his-teeth in each-other, and-got-wet his-clothes, and-got-filthy his-body, and-he-got-scored from (the) walls (of) the-well, and-he-became in a-state hideous.
sentences.i: He fell to shaking like a reed in a gale; his teeth chattered against one another, his clothes were soaked, his body was smeared with filth and scraped raw by the walls of the well, and he was in a shocking state.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to, took to”: yartaʿidu, Form VIII, “to tremble”. rīḥ, “wind”, is feminine, but ʿāṣif, “storming”, keeps the masculine form, as it does in the Qurʾan (rīḥun ʿāṣifun): the Arab grammarians explain it as a word of relation, “a wind possessed of storm”, which need not take the feminine ending. ishtabakat asnānuhu fī baʿḍihā, “his teeth meshed into one another”, the chattering of a man frozen through. ibtallat, Form VIII of balla, “to become wet”. talawwatha, Form V, “to be soiled”. تشطب is read tashaṭṭaba, Form V of shaṭaba, “to score, cut in stripes”, so “to be scratched, grazed”; min gives the cause, the walls of the well. ḥīṭān is the plural of ḥāʾiṭ, “wall”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ صَعُبَ عَلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا رَآهُ فِي تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ṣaʿuba ʿalā Qamari al-Zamāni lammā raʾāhu fī tilka al-ḥālati
sentences.l: So-at that, it-was-hard on Qamar al-Zamān when he-saw-him in that the-state.
sentences.i: Then it grieved Qamar al-Zamān to see him in that condition.
sentences.n: ṣaʿuba ʿalā, “to be hard on”, here in the sense “to distress, move to pity”: the thing that is hard is left unsaid, the sight itself. lammā, “when”, here shades into “because”. The hamza and madda of رآه are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْخَادِمُ نَفْسَهُ عَلَى وَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ قَالَ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدِي دَعْنِي أَرُوحُ وَأَقْلَعُ ثِيَابِي وَأَعْصِرُهَا وَأَنْشُرُهَا فِى الشَّمْسِ وَأَلْبَسُ غَيْرَهَا ثُمَّ أَحْضُرُ إِلَيْكَ سَرِيعًا وَأُخْبِرُكَ بِالْخَبَرِ الصَّحِيحِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-khādimu nafsahu ʿalā wajhi al-arḍi qāla lahu yā sayyidī daʿnī arūḥu wa-aqlaʿu thiyābī wa-aʿṣiruhā wa-anshuruhā fī al-shamsi wa-albasu ghayrahā thumma aḥḍuru ilayka sarīʿan wa-ukhbiruka bi-al-khabari al-ṣaḥīḥi
sentences.l: So-when saw the-servant himself on (the) face (of) the-earth, he-said to-him: O-my-master, let-me go, and-I-strip-off my-clothes and-wring-them and-spread-them in the-sun and-put-on other-than-them; then I-come to-you quickly and-tell-you with-the-news the-true.
sentences.i: When the servant found himself back on the face of the earth, he said to him, “My master, let me go and take off my clothes and wring them out and spread them in the sun, and put on others; then I will come back to you quickly and tell you the true story.”
sentences.n: The print has الاوض, a misprint for الارض, corrected here: al-arḍ, “the earth”. raʾā nafsahu, “he saw himself”: nafs with a suffix is the reflexive, “himself”. daʿnī, imperative of wadaʿa, “let me”. The verbs that follow are plain imperfects, arūḥu, aqlaʿu and the rest, a string of things he will do, where Classical Arabic would put the first in the jussive as the answer to the imperative. rāḥa, “to go”, is the everyday verb of later Arabic. qalaʿa thiyābahu, “to pull off one's clothes”, is likewise the later idiom. ḥaḍara ilā, “to come to, present oneself before”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَاعَبْدَ السُّوءِ لَوْلَا أَنَّكَ عَايَنْتَ الْمَوْتَ مَا أَقْرَرْتَ بِالْحَقِّ وَمَا قُلْتَ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni yā ʿabda al-sūʾi lawlā annaka ʿāyanta al-mawta mā aqrarta bi-al-ḥaqqi wa-mā qulta dhālika
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: O-slave (of) the-evil, were-it-not that-you saw-with-your-eyes the-death, not you-would-have-confessed with-the-truth and-not you-would-have-said that.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “You wretched slave! Had you not looked death in the face, you would never have owned to the truth or said as much.
sentences.n: The print runs يا and عبد together, ياعبد; the spacing is kept. ʿabd al-sūʾ, “slave of evil”, that is, “wicked slave”: the genitive does the work of an adjective. lawlā anna, “were it not that”, followed by the answer, a perfect negated with mā, mā aqrarta; as in Classical Arabic, the la- that a positive answer takes is usually left out after mā. aqarra bi-, Form IV, “to confess, own to”: the verb takes its object with bi-.

sentences.t: فَاخْرُجْ لِقَضَاءِ أَغْرَاضِكَ وَعُدْ إِلَيَّ سَرِيعًا وَأَخْبِرْنِي عَلَى الصَّحِيحِ
sentences.tr: fa-ukhruj li-qaḍāʾi aghrāḍika wa-ʿud ilayya sarīʿan wa-akhbirnī ʿalā al-ṣaḥīḥi
sentences.l: So-go-out for-(the)-settling (of) your-purposes, and-return to-me quickly, and-tell-me according-to the-true-(account).
sentences.i: Go out, then, and see to what you need, and come back to me quickly and tell me the truth.”
sentences.n: li-qaḍāʾi aghrāḍika, “to settle your concerns”: li- gives the purpose, and qaḍāʾ al-gharaḍ, “fulfilling one's need”, is the common phrase for seeing to one's affairs. ʿud, imperative of ʿāda, “to return”. The shadda of اليّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ خَرَجَ الْعَبْدُ وَهُوَ لَايُصَدِّقُ بِالنَّجَاةِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَجْرِي وَيَقَعُ وَيَقُومُ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ أَبِي قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika kharaja al-ʿabdu wa-huwa lā yuṣaddiqu bi-al-najāti wa-lam yazal yajrī wa-yaqaʿu wa-yaqūmu ilā an dakhala ʿalā al-maliki Shahramāna abī Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: So-at that went-out the-slave, and-he not believing in-the-escape; and-not he-ceased running and-falling and-rising, until that he-entered upon the-King Shahramān, (the) father (of) Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: At that the slave went out, scarcely believing he had escaped, and ran on, falling and picking himself up again, until he came in to King Shahramān, Qamar al-Zamān's father.
sentences.n: The print runs لا and يصدق together, لايصدق; the spacing is kept. ṣaddaqa bi-, Form II, “to believe in”: bi- marks what is believed. lam yazal with an imperfect, “he did not stop doing”. ilā an, “until”, here followed by a perfect. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (a person)”, the regular verb for entering someone's presence. The text now calls the khādim, the servant, an ʿabd, a slave: the two words are used of the same man throughout.

sentences.t: فَرَأٰهُ جَالِسًا وَالْوَزِيرُ بِجَانِبِهِ وَهُمَا يَتَحَدَّثَانِ فِي أَمْرِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾāhu jālisan wa-al-wazīru bi-jānibihi wa-humā yataḥaddathāni fī amri Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-he-saw-him sitting, and-the-vizier at-his-side, and-they-two talking-together about (the) affair (of) Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: He found him sitting with the vizier at his side, the two of them talking over the matter of Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: The print spells raʾāhu as فرأه, with its hamza but without the long alif, and the reading is shown here with a small (dagger) alif. jālisan, “sitting”, is a ḥāl, an accusative describing the state he found him in. bi-jānibihi, “at his side”: bi- of place. yataḥaddathāni, Form VI dual, “the two were talking together”; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: وَالْمَلِكُ يَقُولُ لِلْوَزِيرِ إِنِّي لَمْ أَنَمْ هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ مِنِ اشْتِغَالِ قَلْبِي عَلَى وَلَدِي قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-maliku yaqūlu li-al-wazīri innī lam anam hādhihi al-laylata mini ishtighāli qalbī ʿalā waladī Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-the-king saying to-the-vizier: Indeed-I not I-slept this the-night from (the) preoccupation (of) my-heart over my-son Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: The king was saying to the vizier, “I have not slept this night, my heart has been so taken up with my son Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: lam anam, jussive of nāma, “to sleep”, with the long vowel shortened in the closed syllable. hādhihi al-laylata, “this night”, an adverbial accusative of time. ishtighāl al-qalb ʿalā, “the heart's being occupied over”, means anxiety for someone; min gives the cause.

sentences.t: وَإِنِّي أَخَافُ أَنْ يَحْصُلَ لَهُ ضَرَرٌ فِي هٰذَا الْبُرْجِ الْعَتِيقِ وَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ كَانَ فِي سَجْنِهِ مِنَ الْمَصْلَحَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-innī akhāfu an yaḥṣula lahu ḍararun fī hādhā al-burji al-ʿatīqi wa-ayyu shayʾin kāna fī sajnihi mina al-maṣlaḥati
sentences.l: And-indeed-I fear that befalls to-him harm in this the-tower the-old; and-what thing was in his-imprisoning of the-benefit?
sentences.i: I am afraid some harm may come to him in that old tower. And what good was there ever in shutting him up?”
sentences.n: ḥaṣala li-, “to happen to, befall”: li- marks the one it befalls. burj, “tower”. ayyu shayʾin … mina al-maṣlaḥa, “what thing of benefit”: min picks out the kind, “what benefit at all”. سجنه is read sajnihi, the verbal noun, “his imprisoning”; sijnihi, “his prison”, is also possible from the letters. The ء of شيء is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ لَاتَخَفْ عَلَيْهِ وَاللَّهِ لَا يُصِيبُهُ شَيْءٌ أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru lā takhaf ʿalayhi wa-Allāhi lā yuṣībuhu shayʾun abadan
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-vizier: Not fear over-him; by-God, not will-strike-him a-thing ever.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “Have no fear for him. By God, nothing will ever happen to him.
sentences.n: The print runs لا and تخف together, لاتخف; the spacing is kept. lā takhaf, the prohibition, lā with the jussive of khāfa, “to fear”. khāfa ʿalā, “to fear for”: ʿalā marks the one feared for. aṣāba, Form IV, “to strike, befall”.

sentences.t: فَاتْرُكْهُ مَسْجُونًا شَهْرَ زَمَانٍ حَتَّى تَلِينَ عَرِيكَتُهُ وَتَنْكَسِرَ نَفْسُهُ وَيَهْدِيَ خُلْقُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-utrukhu masjūnan shahra zamānin ḥattā talīna ʿarīkatuhu wa-tankasira nafsuhu wa-yahdiya khulquhu
sentences.l: So-leave-him imprisoned a-month (of) time, until softens his-temper, and-breaks his-spirit, and-calms his-disposition.
sentences.i: Leave him shut up for a month's time, until his stubbornness softens, his spirit is broken and his temper is calmed.”
sentences.n: masjūnan, “imprisoned”, passive participle, accusative as a ḥāl. shahra zamānin, “a month of time”, a later idiom for “a full month”, adverbial accusative. lānat ʿarīkatuhu, “his temper became soft”: ʿarīka is a man's natural grain, and layyin al-ʿarīka, “soft of grain”, is a docile person. inkasarat nafsuhu, Form VII, “his pride was broken”. يهدي stands for yahdaʾa, “to grow calm”, from hadaʾa: the hamza has gone and the verb is spelled and said as if from a weak root, as in later speech. It is vocalised yahdiya, subjunctive after ḥattā like its two companions. khulq, “character, temper”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُمَا فِى الْكَلَامِ وَإِذَا بِالْخَادِمِ دَخَلَ عَلَيْهِمَا وَهُوَ فِي تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ فَانْزَعَجَ الْمَلِكُ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā fī al-kalāmi wa-idhā bi-al-khādimi dakhala ʿalayhimā wa-huwa fī tilka al-ḥālati fa-inzaʿaja al-maliku minhu
sentences.l: And-while they-two (were) in the-talk, and-behold, the-servant entered upon-them-two, and-he (was) in that the-state; so-was-alarmed the-king from-him.
sentences.i: While they were talking, in came the servant upon them, still in that sorry state, and the king was alarmed at the sight of him.
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā, “while … behold”: the narrator's set way of bringing in a surprise. Classical Arabic would say idhā without the wāw. After idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears, bi-al-khādimi, “behold, the servant”. inzaʿaja, Form VII, “to be alarmed, disturbed”; min gives the cause.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْخَادِمُ يَا مَوْلَانَا السُّلْطَانَ إِنَّ وَلَدَكَ طَارَ عَقْلُهُ وَصَارَ مَجْنُونًا وَقَدْ فَعَلَ بِي كَذَا وَكَذَا حَتَّى صِرْتُ كَمَا تَرَانِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-khādimu yā mawlānā al-sulṭāna inna waladaka ṭāra ʿaqluhu wa-ṣāra majnūnan wa-qad faʿala bī kadhā wa-kadhā ḥattā ṣirtu kamā tarānī
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-servant: O our-lord the-sultan, indeed your-son, has-flown his-mind, and-he-has-become mad; and-he-has done with-me so and-so, until I-became as you-see-me.
sentences.i: The servant said to him, “O our lord the sultan, your son has lost his wits and gone mad. He has done such-and-such to me, until I am as you see me now.
sentences.n: yā mawlānā al-sulṭāna, “O our lord the sultan”, the court's form of address; al-sulṭāna follows mawlānā in the accusative. inna waladaka ṭāra ʿaqluhu, literally “your son, his mind has flown”: the topic comes first and the suffix -hu picks it up. faʿala bi-, “to do (something) to”: bi- marks the person it is done to. kadhā wa-kadhā, “such and such”, the narrator's shorthand for an account the reader already knows.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ يَقُولُ لِي إِنَّ صَبِيَّةً بَاتَتْ عِنْدِي فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَذَهَبَتْ بِخُفْيَةٍ فَأَيْنَ هِيَ وَيُكَلِّفُنِى أَنِّي أُخْبِرُهُ لَهَا وَبِمَنْ أَخَذَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-huwa yaqūlu lī inna ṣabiyyatan bātat ʿindī fī hādhihi al-laylati wa-dhahabat bi-khufyatin fa-ayna hiya wa-yukallifunī annī ukhbiruhu lahā wa-bi-man akhadhahā
sentences.l: And-he saying to-me: Indeed a-girl spent-the-night with-me in this the-night and-went-away in-secret; so-where (is) she? And-he-charges-me that-I tell-him of-her, and-about-who took-her.
sentences.i: He keeps saying to me, ‘A girl spent the night with me this very night and slipped away in secret, so where is she?’ And he is pressing me to tell him about her, and who it was that took her.
sentences.n: bāta, “to spend the night”. bi-khufyatin, “in secret”: bi- of manner. kallafa, Form II, “to charge, put (someone) to a task”; Classical Arabic would follow it with an and the subjunctive, but here it takes annī, “that I”, and a plain imperfect, ukhbiruhu, a later construction that recurs. The rest of the sentence is loose and the reading is uncertain. akhbara usually marks the news with bi-, and the speaker seems to start with lahā, “about her”, then switch to bi-man akhadhahā, “of who took her”. ‘Who took her’ is the likeliest sense, though bi-man could also be read “by means of whom”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا لَارَأَيْتُ صَبِيَّةً وَلَا صَبِيًّا وَالْبَابُ طُولَ اللَّيْلِ مَغْلُوقٌ وَأَنَا نَائِمٌ عَلَى بَابِهِ وَالْمِفْتَاحُ تَحْتَ رَأْسِي وَفَتَحْتُ لَهُ فِى الصُّبْحِ بِيَدِي
sentences.tr: wa-anā lā raʾaytu ṣabiyyatan wa-lā ṣabiyyan wa-al-bābu ṭūla al-layli maghlūqun wa-anā nāʾimun ʿalā bābihi wa-al-miftāḥu taḥta raʾsī wa-fataḥtu lahu fī al-ṣubḥi bi-yadī
sentences.l: And-I, not I-saw a-girl and-not a-boy; and-the-door (the) length (of) the-night (was) locked, and-I sleeping at his-door, and-the-key under my-head; and-I-opened for-him in the-morning with-my-hand.
sentences.i: But I have seen neither girl nor boy. The door was locked all night long, and I was asleep at his door with the key under my head, and I opened it for him myself in the morning.”
sentences.n: The print runs لا and رأيت together, لارأيت; the spacing is kept, and the hamza of رأيت is printed. lā raʾaytu … wa-lā, “I saw neither … nor”: Classical Arabic does use lā with the perfect when it is repeated like this, though mā raʾaytu is the plain past denial. ṭūla al-layli, “all night long”, an adverbial accusative. maghlūq, “locked”, for Classical mughlaq: the later language makes the participle from the plain verb ghalaqa. bi-yadī, “with my own hand”: bi- of the instrument. The ئ of نائم and the hamza of رأسي are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ عَنْ وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ صَرَخَ قَائِلًا وَاوَلَدَاهْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku Shahramānu hādhā al-kalāma ʿan waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni ṣarakha qāʾilan wā-waladāh
sentences.l: So-when heard the-King Shahramān these the-words about his-son Qamar al-Zamān, he-cried-out saying: Alas-my-son!
sentences.i: When King Shahramān heard this said of his son Qamar al-Zamān, he cried aloud, “Alas, my son!”
sentences.n: qāʾilan, “saying”, active participle in the accusative as a ḥāl; its ئ is printed. wā-waladāh, “O my son, alas!”, is the nudba, the cry of lament: wā- before the name of the one mourned, and a long -ā with a pausal -h after it.

sentences.t: وَغَضِبَ عَلَى الْوَزِيرِ الَّذِي كَانَ سَبَبًا فِي هٰذِهِ الْأُمُورِ غَضَبًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: wa-ghaḍiba ʿalā al-wazīri alladhī kāna sababan fī hādhihi al-umūri ghaḍaban shadīdan
sentences.l: And-he-was-angry at the-vizier who was a-cause in these the-matters, an-anger severe.
sentences.i: And he was furious with the vizier, who had been the cause of all this.
sentences.n: ghaḍiba ʿalā, “to be angry with”: ʿalā marks the one at whom the anger is aimed. ghaḍaban shadīdan, “with a fierce anger”, the cognate accusative, repeating the verb as a noun to say how hard he was angry. It was the vizier who had advised shutting Qamar al-Zamān in the tower. umūr, plural of amr, “matter”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ قُمِ اكْشِفْ لِي خَبَرَ وَلَدِي وَانْظُرْ مَا جَرَى فِي عَقْلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu qumi ikshif lī khabara waladī wa-unẓur mā jarā fī ʿaqlihi
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Rise, uncover for-me (the) news (of) my-son, and-look-at what has-happened in his-mind.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Get up, find out for me how it is with my son, and see what has come over his mind.”
sentences.n: qumi ikshif, “get up and find out”, with a helping -i before the joining alif: two imperatives side by side with no “and”, as in speech. kashafa, “to uncover”, here “to look into”; lī, “for me”, the one the service is done for. jarā, “to run, happen”.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْوَزِيرُ وَخَرَجَ وَهُوَ يَتَعَثَّرُ فِي أَذْيَالِهِ مِنْ خَوْفِهِ مِنْ سَطْوَةِ الْمَلِكِ وَرَاحَ مَعَ الْخَادِمِ إِلَى الْبُرْجِ وَكَانَتِ الشَّمْسُ قَدْ طَلَعَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-wazīru wa-kharaja wa-huwa yataʿaththaru fī adhyālihi min khawfihi min saṭwati al-maliki wa-rāḥa maʿa al-khādimi ilā al-burji wa-kānati al-shamsu qad ṭalaʿat
sentences.l: So-rose the-vizier and-went-out, and-he stumbling in his-skirts from his-fear of (the) wrath (of) the-king; and-he-went with the-servant to the-tower, and-the-sun had already risen.
sentences.i: So the vizier rose and went out, tripping over his skirts for fear of the king's wrath, and went with the servant to the tower; and by now the sun had risen.
sentences.n: taʿaththara fī adhyālihi, “to stumble in one's skirts”, the stock picture of a man hurrying in fright: adhyāl is the plural of dhayl, the trailing hem of a robe. The first min gives the cause, his fear; the second the thing feared. saṭwa, “assault, overbearing power”. kānat … qad ṭalaʿat, “had risen”, kāna with qad and a perfect gives the pluperfect.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ الْوَزِيرُ عَلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فَوَجَدَهُ جَالِسًا عَلَى السَّرِيرِ يَقْرَأُ الْقُرْآنَ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala al-wazīru ʿalā Qamari al-Zamāni fa-wajadahu jālisan ʿalā al-sarīri yaqraʾu al-qurʾāna
sentences.l: So-entered the-vizier upon Qamar al-Zamān and-found-him sitting on the-couch reading the-Qurʾan.
sentences.i: The vizier went in to Qamar al-Zamān and found him sitting on his couch, reading the Qurʾan.
sentences.n: wajada, “to find”, with two objects, the person and the state he is in: jālisan, then yaqraʾu, a second ḥāl as a clause. sarīr, “couch, bed”. The hamza of يقرأ and القرآن is printed.

sentences.t: فَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ الْوَزِيرُ وَجَلَسَ إِلَى جَانِبِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدِي إِنَّ هٰذَا الْخَادِمَ السُّوءَ أَخْبَرَنَا بِخَبَرٍ شَوَّشَ عَلَيْنَا وَأَزْعَجَنَا فَاغْتَاظَ الْمَلِكُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-sallama ʿalayhi al-wazīru wa-jalasa ilā jānibihi wa-qāla lahu yā sayyidī inna hādhā al-khādima al-sūʾa akhbaranā bi-khabarin shawwasha ʿalaynā wa-azʿajanā fa-ightāẓa al-maliku min dhālika
sentences.l: So-greeted him the-vizier and-sat to his-side and-said to-him: O-my-master, indeed this the-servant the-evil told-us with-news (that) confused on-us and-alarmed-us, so-was-enraged the-king from that.
sentences.i: The vizier greeted him and sat down beside him, and said to him, “My master, this wretched servant has brought us a story that has thrown us into confusion and alarm, and the king is enraged at it.”
sentences.n: sallama ʿalā, Form II, “to greet (with al-salāmu ʿalaykum)”: ʿalā marks the one greeted; its shadda is printed, as is that of ياسيّدي, which the print again runs together. al-khādima al-sūʾa, “the bad servant”: here sūʾ, “evil”, is used as a plain adjective after the noun, where Classical Arabic would say khādim al-sūʾ, as with ʿabd al-sūʾ above. shawwasha ʿalā, Form II, “to throw into confusion, upset”: ʿalā marks the one upset. ightāẓa, Form VIII, “to be enraged”; min gives the cause.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَمَا الَّذِي قَالَ لَكُمْ عَنِّى حَتَّى شَوَّشَ عَلَٰي أَبِي وَفِى الْحَقِيقَةِ هُوَ مَا شَوَّشَ إِلَّا عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-mā alladhī qāla lakum ʿannī ḥattā shawwasha ʿalā abī wa-fī al-ḥaqīqati huwa mā shawwasha illā ʿalayya
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: And-what (is) that-which he-said to-you about-me, so-that he-upset (on) my-father? And-in the-truth, he not upset except (on) me.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “And what is it he told you about me, that he has so upset my father? In truth, it is no one but me he has upset.”
sentences.n: wa-mā alladhī, “and what is it that”: mā, “what”, with a relative clause. ḥattā here gives the result, “so that”. In the first علي the print spells ʿalā with a final ي; the reading ʿalā is shown with a small (dagger) alif. In the second, عليّ, the shadda is printed and the word is ʿalayya, “me”. mā … illā, “not … except”, gives “only”: “it is only me he has upset”. The shaddas of شوّش and الّا are printed, and so is the ى of عنّى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ إِنَّهُ جَاءَ إِلَيْنَا بِحَالَةٍ مُنْكَرَةٍ وَقَالَ لِوَالِدِكَ قَوْلًا حَاشَاكَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru innahu jāʾa ilaynā bi-ḥālatin munkaratin wa-qāla li-wālidika qawlan ḥāshāka minhu
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-vizier: Indeed-he came to-us in-a-state shocking, and-said to-your-father a-saying, far-be-you from-it.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “He came to us in a dreadful state and said something to your father that could never be true of you,
sentences.n: bi-ḥālatin, “in a state”: bi- of accompanying circumstance. munkar, passive participle of Form IV, “disapproved of, shocking”. ḥāshāka minhu, “you are far exempt from it”: ḥāshā, “far be it”, a courtier's way of disowning the charge even as he reports it.

sentences.t: وَكَذَبَ عَلَيْنَا هٰذَا الْعَبْدُ بِمَا لَايَنْبَغِي أَنْ يُذْكَرَ فِي شَأْنِكَ فَسَلَامَةُ شَبَابِكَ وَسَلَامَةُ عَقْلِكَ الرَّجِيحِ وَلِسَانِكَ الْفَصِيحِ وَحَاشَا أَنْ يَظْهَرَ مِنْكَ قَبِيحٌ
sentences.tr: wa-kadhaba ʿalaynā hādhā al-ʿabdu bi-mā lā yanbaghī an yudhkara fī shaʾnika fa-salāmatu shabābika wa-salāmatu ʿaqlika al-rajīḥi wa-lisānika al-faṣīḥi wa-ḥāshā an yaẓhara minka qabīḥun
sentences.l: And-lied to-us this the-slave with-what not is-fitting that it-be-mentioned in your-regard. So-(the)-soundness (of) your-youth, and-(the)-soundness (of) your-mind the-weighty and-your-tongue the-eloquent! And-far-be-it that should-appear from-you an-ugly-(thing).
sentences.i: and this slave lied to us with things that ought never to be spoken of you. God keep your youth safe, and keep sound your weighty mind and your eloquent tongue! Far be it that anything unseemly should come from you.”
sentences.n: kadhaba ʿalā, “to lie against, lie to”: ʿalā marks the one lied to. bi-mā, “with what”: bi- marks the content of the lie. The print runs لا and ينبغي together, لاينبغي; the spacing is kept. fī shaʾnika, “concerning you”; the hamza of شأنك is printed. The words fa-salāmatu shabābika … are a wish of the kind “may your youth be kept safe”, set in the nominative with nothing to govern them; one could also take them as an oath, “by the soundness of your youth”, but the print gives no bi-. The vizier's flattery falls into rhymed prose: rajīḥ, “weighty”, faṣīḥ, “eloquent”, qabīḥ, “ugly”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ فَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ قَالَهُ هٰذَا الْعَبْدُ النَّحْسُ عَنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni ayyuhā al-wazīru fa-ayyu shayʾin qālahu hādhā al-ʿabdu al-naḥsu ʿannī
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: O vizier, so-what thing said-it this the-slave the-ill-omened about-me?
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “Vizier, what was it, then, that this ill-omened slave said of me?”
sentences.n: ayyuhā al-wazīru, “O vizier”, a vocative without yā. qālahu, “he said it”: the suffix -hu takes up ayyu shayʾin, “what thing”. naḥs, properly a noun, “ill luck”, is used here as an adjective, “ill-omened, wretched”, a common term of abuse. The shaddas of ايّها, فايّ and عنّي are printed, and so is the ء of شيء.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ إِنَّهُ أَخْبَرَنَا أَنَّ عَقْلَكَ ذَهَبَ وَقُلْتَ لَهُ إِنَّهُ كَانَ عِنْدَكَ صَبِيَّةٌ فِى اللَّيْلَةِ الْمَاضِيَةِ وَكَلَّفْتَهُ أَنَّهُ يُخْبِرُكَ أَيْنَ ذَهَبَتْ وَعَذَّبْتَهُ عَلَى ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru innahu akhbaranā anna ʿaqlaka dhahaba wa-qulta lahu innahu kāna ʿindaka ṣabiyyatun fī al-laylati al-māḍiyati wa-kallaftahu annahu yukhbiruka ayna dhahabat wa-ʿadhdhabtahu ʿalā dhālika
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-vizier: Indeed-he told-us that your-mind went, and-you-said to-him: Indeed-it was with-you a-girl in the-night the-past; and-you-charged-him that-he tell-you where she-went, and-you-tormented-him over that.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “He told us that your wits had gone, and that you said to him there had been a girl with you last night, and pressed him to tell you where she had gone, and tormented him over it.”
sentences.n: innahu kāna ʿindaka ṣabiyyatun, “that there was with you a girl”: the -hu of innahu is the pronoun of the situation, standing for “the fact is”, and the verb kāna stays masculine because it is separated from its feminine subject. After qāla, inna is used, not anna. kallaftahu annahu yukhbiruka, “you charged him that he should tell you”: again kallafa with anna and a plain imperfect, as the servant said it. ʿadhdhaba ʿalā, Form II, “to torment (someone) over”: ʿalā gives the grounds. The shaddas of انّ, صبيّة, كلّفته and عذّبته are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ اغْتَاظَ غَيْظًا شَدِيدًا وَقَالَ لِلْوَزِيرِ تَبَيَّنَ لِي أَنَّكُمْ عَلَّمْتُمُ الْخَادِمَ الْفِعْلَ الَّذِي صَدَرَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Qamaru al-Zamāni hādhā al-kalāma ightāẓa ghayẓan shadīdan wa-qāla li-al-wazīri tabayyana lī annakum ʿallamtumu al-khādima al-fiʿla alladhī ṣadara minhu
sentences.l: So-when heard Qamar al-Zamān these the-words, he-was-enraged a-rage severe, and-said to-the-vizier: It-has-become-clear to-me that-you (pl.) taught the-servant the-deed that issued from-him.
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān heard this he flew into a violent rage, and said to the vizier, “It is plain to me that you people put the servant up to what he did.
sentences.n: ightāẓa ghayẓan shadīdan, “he raged a fierce rage”, the cognate accusative again. tabayyana li-, Form V, “to become clear to”: li- marks the one to whom it is clear. ʿallama, Form II, takes two objects, the one taught and the thing taught: “you taught the servant the deed”. ʿallamtum takes a helping u before the article, ʿallamtumu al-. ṣadara min, “to issue from”, a formal way of saying “what he did”. The plural -kum takes in the king and the vizier together. The shaddas of تبيّن and علّمتم are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. Here the print sets the name as one word, شهرزاد.
